newsitem.title: UK: UK share buyback rule makes more room for tax cuts. [CORRECTED 10:56 GMT]
newsitem.headline: UK share buyback rule makes more room for tax cuts. [CORRECTED 10:56 GMT]

text.p: The UK Treasury's decision to cancel tax credits on share buybacks announced on Tuesday will give the country's coffers a timely boost and make more room for Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to cut income tax in the November budget, analysts said.
Clarke said the change would produce an estimated yield for the Exchequer of up to 400 million stg.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), a leading think-tank, said at first glance the total savings seemed greater, but given the ruling does not cover some key special dividends, the Exchequer's estimate appears correct. (Corrects following clarification from the IFS, taking into account the full details of the ruling.)
City estimates suggest share buybacks and special dividend payouts could top 4.0 billion stg this year, up from 1.0 billion stg last year.
But the ruling allows investors to still claim tax credits on some special dividends, mostly those unrelated to takeover activity or share consolidation, and reduces the Exchequer's saving.
The announcement, just weeks away from the November budget, should give Chancellor Clarke a little more elbow room to make the income tax cuts which some party colleagues are urging him to do.
David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan, forecasts Chancellor Clarke may cut up to three pence off the 24 percent standard rate of income tax.

"The Treasury is looking for anything that will help it reduce income tax without denting the PSBR profile. Tax cuts will be paid for through stronger economic growth next year, trimming back public spending relative to existing plans, and if the Treasury can find any other tax breaks to withdraw, it will," Mackie said. Some analysts expect profit-related pay may be next for the chop.
But he expects the budget to contain enough spending cuts to match any income tax cuts.
"Britain will look very out on a limb if its budget looks expansionary while the rest of Europe pushes through Draconion measures to reduce their deficits."
